Received 1993 September 29; in original form 1993 March 24 SUMMARY The Upper Carboniferous-Lower Triassic Pyongan Supergroup is exposed in an E-W trending syncline comprising the Samcheok Coalfield in eastern South Korea; it borders the southern margin of a NE-SW trending (Okcheon) zone of Upper Jurassic-Lower Cretaceous deformation (Daebo Orogeny). Although a Recent field overprint widely recorded in Korean rocks is represented here, an ancient field component structure is recovered from the red bed facies in this Supergroup by detailed thermal demagnetization. A prominent Upper Jurassic-Cretaceous over- print is widespread (DIZ = 56.1/54.8", agS = 9.6", palaeopole at 200.4"E, 46.7"N) and records the magnetic effect of the Daebo Orogeny within the Okcheon Belt. It is post-deformational in origin and appears to have been confined mainly to the Cretaceous Normal Superchron. It has been rotated clockwise since these times, in common with the main synclinal axis, as a consequence of dextral movements along the Tan Lu Fault System. The Tosagok Formation is dated as Kazanian (Lee 1987) and was therefore probably deposited slightly before the end of the Carboniferous-Permian Reversed (CPR) Super- chron. The concensus of present evidence places the end of this superchron between Lower and Upper Tartarian times, or within the Upper Tartarian stage (Molina-Garza, Geissman & Van der Voo 1989; Harland et al. 1990). Hence the presence of reversals in the hbt (haematite-resident) components of the Tosagok Formation is indicative of remanence acquisition somewhat later than deposition, and implies a post-depositional or early diagenetic origin. The succession in this area is summarized in Table 1 and unconformably overlies (Lower Cambrian to Middle Ordovician) rocks belonging to the Choseon Supergroup. It commences with red or drab detrital sediments of the Manhang Formation ranging from siltstones to fine-pebble conglomerates; samples from the red facies comprise an important component of this study (Table 1). Received 1993 September 29; in original form 1993 March 24 SUMMARY The Upper Carboniferous-Lower Triassic Pyongan Supergroup is exposed in an E-W trending syncline comprising the Samcheok Coalfield in eastern South Korea; it borders the southern margin of a NE-SW trending (Okcheon) zone of Upper Jurassic-Lower Cretaceous deformation (Daebo Orogeny). Although a Recent field overprint widely recorded in Korean rocks is represented here, an ancient field component structure is recovered from the red bed facies in this Supergroup by detailed thermal demagnetization. A prominent Upper Jurassic-Cretaceous over- print is widespread (DIZ = 56.1/54.8", agS = 9.6", palaeopole at 200.4"E, 46.7"N) and records the magnetic effect of the Daebo Orogeny within the Okcheon Belt. It is post-deformational in origin and appears to have been confined mainly to the Cretaceous Normal Superchron. It has been rotated clockwise since these times, in common with the main synclinal axis, as a consequence of dextral movements along the Tan Lu Fault System. The field cores were trimmed into 2.2cm long cylinders for subsequent palaeomagnetic analysis. 3 PALAEOMAGNETIC RESULTS All samples were subjected to progressive thermal demagnetization and measured at each stage of treatment by cryogenic magnetometer. Heating steps were 100 "C to 300"C, then in 50°C steps to 5OO0C, and subsequently in 20 "C steps up to the Curie points of the remanence carriers; the heatings were made by a Magnetic Measurements thermal demagnetizer and all experimental work was undertaken in a continuously monitored field free space provided by a set of large Rubens coils. The effects of thermal treatment were monitored at each stage of treatment by making susceptibility measurements; no significant chemical changes were identified in the samples (mostly red beds) yielding significant components of magnetization. section_candidates.excerpt: Earth and Planetary Science Letters, 117 (1993) 525-552 525 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V., Amsterdam [PT] Paleomagnetic study of Permian and Mesozoic sedimentary rocks from Northern Thailand supports the extrusion model for Indochina Zhenyu Yang and Jean Besse Laboratoire de Pal~omagn~tisme, Institut de Physique du Globe de Paris, 4 place Jussieu, Tour 24, 1 e ~tage, 75252 Paris C~dex 05, France Received November 23, 1992; revision accepted March 26, 1993 ABSTRACT The mode of deformation of southeast Asia resulting from the Indian collision is still controversial: is convergence between stable India and Siberia absorbed principally by crustal shortening and thickening and minor strike-slip faulting or by a mechanism of extrusion involving crustal thickening and lateral escape of blocks along major strike-slip zones? In order to test these models, we have carried out a paleomagnetic study of sedimentary rocks of Jurassic to Cretaceous age on the Khorat Plateau in Thailand. A large discrepancy between the poles of Indochina presented in this paper and a compilation of South China block pole positions both at the Triassic/

sented in this paper and a compilation of South China block pole positions both at the Triassic/Jurassic and the Jurassic/Cretaceous boundary imply some 1500 +_ 800 km of post-middle Cretaceous left-lateral slip along the Red River and Xian Shui He fault zones and approximately 14 + 7 ° of clockwise rotation for the Indochina block relative to the South China block. Such relative motions are in agreement with a model of lateral extrusion of Indochina during the India-Asia collision. Additional data of Permian, Upper Triassic and Lower Jurassic age collected in Indochina indicate a post-late Permian remagnetization for the upper Permian limestones. A comparison of these data with those from Yunnan (South China), the North China block and the South China block shows that these blocks have probably been in contact at least since the late Triassic. I. Introduction The India-Asia collision has significantly af- fected the Cretaceous landscape of central and southeastern Asia since the beginning of the Ter- tiary (Fig. la). As a result, the geological history of the assembly of the different blocks involved in the pre-Tertiary collision is still a matter of heated debate. The Indochina block, for example, is con- sidered to have collided with the South China block in the Tourna

lision are also strongly debated. The conver- gence between stable India and Eurasia (or Siberia), which is in excess of 2600 km [7-10], is, according to England and Houseman [11], ab- sorbed principally by crustal shortening and thickening and minor strike-slip faulting, while Tapponnier and Molnar [12], Tapponnier et al. [10] and Peltzer and Tapponnier [13] argue for a mechanism involving crustal thickening and lat- eral escape of blocks along major strike-slip zones (the extrusion model). In this controversial con- text, paleomagnetic studies can provide an inde- pendent tool to constrain the paleogeographic history and the deformation mode of these blocks. 0012-821X/93/$06.00 © 1993 - Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. Previous paleomagnetic studies on the Khorat plateau The paleomagnetic data on the Indochina block and Shan-Thai block obtained in the 1970's and the beginning of 1980's are in general of poor quality [32-34]. Indeed, although some thermal demagnetizations in pilot studies were carried out 528 Z. YANG AND J. BESSE up to 600°C, most of the samples were routinely demagnetized to temperatures never exceeding 200-300°C, a rather low temperature for separat- ing components often carried by hematite and sometimes by both magnetite and hematite. Moreover, most of these results were based on a small number of sites or samples. More recently, a preliminary paleomagnetic study of upper Tri- assic rocks from the western Khorat basin (Northeast Thailand) was carried out by Achache and Courtillot [23], and provided an upper Trias- sic pole for the Khorat plateau. In the region of the west Kho- rat basin, the Indosinian orogeny is marked by the unconformity of the Mesozoic succession over a strongly folded marine limestone succession of upper Permian age, which has been well dated by a rich Fusulina fauna [27,28]. Possible unconformities are also diffi- cult to establish. Recent progress in vertebrate paleontology has led to more precise definition of the stratigraphic ages, however [29]. Large continental basins of the same age can also be found in central Yunnan and Sichuan (Fig. la). The Khorat Group is usually divided into sev- eral formations based on lithostratigraphic cycles. However, sparse fossils (mostly wood and plant material) and poor exposure have led to dit'ficul- ties in dating, dividing and establishing a full sequence. Possible unconformities are also diffi- cult to establish. Recent progress in vertebrate paleontology has led to more precise definition of the stratigraphic ages, however [29]. The lower- most formation of the Mesozoic Khorat Group, the Huai Hin Lat Formation, consists of a succes- sion of limestones and sandstones and contains a rich freshwater vertebrate fauna (e.g., fishes, ste- gocephalians, turtles and phytosaura). The as- signed age is Norian (late Triassic). This succes- sion is conformably overlain by a red siltstone formation (the Nam Phong Formation), which has been assigned a post-Norian-pre-middle Jurassic age. This succession is overlain by the Phu Kradung Formation, which includes various vertebrates, such as the crocodilian Sunosuchus thailandicus of middle Jurassic age [6]. The Khorat Group is usually divided into sev- eral formations based on lithostratigraphic cycles. However, sparse fossils (mostly wood and plant material) and poor exposure have led to dit'ficul- ties in dating, dividing and establishing a full sequence. Possible unconformities are also diffi- cult to establish. Recent progress in vertebrate paleontology has led to more precise definition of the stratigraphic ages, however [29]. The lower- most formation of the Mesozoic Khorat Group, the Huai Hin Lat Formation, consists of a succes- sion of limestones and sandstones and contains a rich freshwater vertebrate fauna (e.g., fishes, ste- gocephalians, turtles and phytosaura). The as- signed age is Norian (late Triassic). This succes- sion is conformably overlain by a red siltstone formation (the Nam Phong Formation), which has been assigned a post-Norian-pre-middle Jurassic age. This succession is overlain by the Phu Kradung Formation, which includes various vertebrates, such as the crocodilian Sunosuchus thailandicus of middle Jurassic age [6]. a. Here we report Cretaceous and Tertiary pale- omagnetic results obtained over a large area in south China from Guangxi, Fujian and Guang- dong provinces (Fig. 1). We then compare the results to an average Cretaceous pole from Sichuan Province. Sichuan is only weakly de- formed, so comparison of the results reported here with those from Sichuan provide insight into the post-Cretaceous deformation of south China. A de- crease in NRM intensity in the interval recording the 313C event was observed in all sections (Figs. 4-6, 8 and 9). otope data are presented from five Lower Cretaceous pelagic limestone sections in the Southern Alps. A positive carbon isotope event is recorded in bulk carbonate from the Upper Valanginian of all five sections, and the magnetostratigraphy and biostratigraphy provide the age model. The record of the isotope event in absolute time is closely replicated in all five sections. As the sections are located in two paleogeographic basins and are separated by up to 300 km, the synchronous isotope event cannot be interpreted as an artifact of diagenesis. A reduction in magnetization intensity coincident with the 613C peak may be due to diagenetic magnetite dissolution enhanced by increased organic carbon burial. According to the age model, which uses GTS89 timescale [1], background ~13C values of 1.5%o are recorded from 145 to 137 Ma. Between 137 and 136 Ma, ~13C increases to a maximum value of about 3%o. Values begin to decrease from 136 Ma and reach background values at about 132 Ma. The rate of change of 613C for the onset of the event (about 1.5%o/m.y.) is greater than for the decay (about 0.5%o/m.y.), suggesting an abrupt perturbation of the carbon system from equilibrium, followed by a more gradual return to background values. 1. To date these are the only well dated rocks of this age in the Tien Shan. Due to their mottled appearance and friability the redbeds were not sampled. Forty-seven hand samples were taken from the other three members, from layers of varying attitude. One hand sample oriented with a magnetic compass was taken at each stratigraphic level at each sampled section, the sampling points being spaced several metres apart along the sections. At each site in sections H1 and H2, six to eight cores were drilled from a sedimentary layer about of about 1 m in thickness; sun and magnetic compasses were used for the orientation of the cores. Treatments Each hand sample was cut into two to four cubic specimens in the field using a portable diamond saw. In the laboratory the cores were cut into standard specimens. The laboratory study was started in the paleomagnetic laboratory in Moscow and was completed in Rennes. Thermal demagnetization of pilot cores was carried out in a home-made oven with an internal residual field of less than 10 nT and measurements were made with a Czechoslovakian JR-4 spinner magnetome- ter. field using a portable diamond saw. In the laboratory the cores were cut into standard specimens. In Rennes, the collection was cleaned in Schonstedt thermal demagnetizer, and Schonst- edt spinner and cryogenic magnetometers were used for measurements. The results were ana- lyzed, as usual, on stereonets and orthogonal diagrams. The statistical treatments were somewhat dif- ferent for the two types of sampling: Two speci- mens from a hand sample were demagnetized and a sample-mean for each identified compo- nent was computed and used for analysis. One specimen from each core was treated and all unit vectors were averaged to obtain the site-mean. Both sample- and site-means were given the same weight during analysis. We identify these where a neighbouring site exhibits three components, and the intermediate component can be equated in direction with the higher T component in the two-component site (e.g., Sites B127 and B128). The high-T component at this site is not well defined, although the end point of the demagnetisation curve is relatively consistent.

e Miocene. This overlaps a period of dextrally oblique convergence during the early to middle Miocene along the Internal/External Zone Boundary and within the External Zone. Rotations in the External Zone are recorded by palaeomagnetic results from 27 sites in Upper Jurassic (Ammonitico rosso facies) limestones from the Subbetic Zone, and one site of a similar age from the Prebetic. The sites show either two- or three-component behaviour. The low-temperature component is coincident with the present-field direction. The intermediate-temperature component was probably acquired during Miocene folding. The high-temperature component passes fold tests (Miocene age) and a conglomerate test (Eocene-early Oligocene age). Palaeomagnetic declinations from individual tectonic blocks in the Subbetic are consistent, but indicate large differential rotations between blocks. The largest rotations occur on relatively small isolated blocks of Jurassic carbonates in a highly deformed Triassic evaporite sequence. [31] have used anisotropy of mag- netic susceptibility (AMS) to demonstrate an early remanence in sediments exhibiting a depositional magnetic fabric. These Tortonian sediments have a typical sedimentary AMS fabric--oblate, with the minimum axis subvertical. The directions of the maximum axes are consistent, with the mean directed towards the northeast, perhaps reflect- ing a dominant current flow direction. The oblate fabric is probably largely a consequence of com- paction. We suggest that the possible presence of a sedimentary fabric is an argument for an early, pre-compaction remanence in these sediments. ]. Site B49 from the Prebetic also exhibits two-component behaviour, on both thermal and AF treatment. A few sites (seven) from the central part of the Subbetic display three-component behaviour--a low-T component, an intermediate-T component (260°C < T< 480°C), and a high-T component (480°C < T < 600°C) (Fig. 3b and Table 1). In a few cases the intermediate component is domi- nant and the high-T component very poorly de- fined. The intermediate component has a con- stant polarity at any single site, and generally has a direction distinctly different from that of the high-T component. AF treatment gives similar results, but the high-coercivity (high-temperature) component is typically poorly resolved. At a few two-component sites we believe that the intermediate component completely obscures the high-T component. We identify these where a neighbouring site exhibits three components, and the intermediate component can be equated in direction with the higher T component in the two-component site (e.g., Sites B127 and B128). Samples from site B37 carry an intermediate component which is anomalously steep and does not decay to the origin. The high-T component at this site is not well defined, although the end point of the demagnetisation curve is relatively consistent.

NRM intensities are relatively high, up to 9 mA/m. The magnetic mineralogy is dominated by a high-coercivity, high-T (650°C) phase, presumably specular haematite [30]. The coarser grained clastic Torto- nian detritus was derived from the Permo-Tri- assic red beds and dolomites that are now ex- posed in the Sierra Espufia; it is likely that red beds were also the origin of the haematite seen in the fine-grained rocks. Thermal demagnetisation reveals clear, stable, north-down directed components (Table 3 and Fig. 5a). As these rocks are not folded, no fold test can be applied, so it is difficult to assess the age of the magnetisation. e Miocene. This overlaps a period of dextrally oblique convergence during the early to middle Miocene along the Internal/External Zone Boundary and within the External Zone. Rotations in the External Zone are recorded by palaeomagnetic results from 27 sites in Upper Jurassic (Ammonitico rosso facies) limestones from the Subbetic Zone, and one site of a similar age from the Prebetic. The sites show either two- or three-component behaviour. The low-temperature component is coincident with the present-field direction. The intermediate-temperature component was probably acquired during Miocene folding. The high-temperature component passes fold tests (Miocene age) and a conglomerate test (Eocene-early Oligocene age). Palaeomagnetic declinations from individual tectonic blocks in the Subbetic are consistent, but indicate large differential rotations between blocks. These blocks are underlain by low-angle thrust faults, which probably accommodated much of the rotation. The largest rotations occur on relatively small isolated blocks of Jurassic carbonates in a highly deformed Triassic evaporite sequence. The rotations occurred after latest Oligocene times, and probably before the late Miocene. This overlaps a period of dextrally oblique convergence during the early to middle Miocene along the Internal/External Zone Boundary and within the External Zone. Rotations in the External Zone are recorded by palaeomagnetic results from 27 sites in Upper Jurassic (Ammonitico rosso facies) limestones from the Subbetic Zone, and one site of a similar age from the Prebetic. The sites show either two- or three-component behaviour. The low-temperature component is coincident with the present-field direction. The intermediate-temperature component was probably acquired during Miocene folding. The high-temperature component passes fold tests (Miocene age) and a conglomerate test (Eocene-early Oligocene age). Palaeomagnetic declinations from individual tectonic blocks in the Subbetic are consistent, but indicate large differential rotations between blocks. These blocks

dent with the present-field direction. The intermediate-temperature component was probably acquired during Miocene folding. The high-temperature component passes fold tests (Miocene age) and a conglomerate test (Eocene-early Oligocene age). Palaeomagnetic declinations from individual tectonic blocks in the Subbetic are consistent, but indicate large differential rotations between blocks. These blocks are underlain by low-angle thrust faults, which probably accommodated much of the rotation. The largest rotations occur on relatively small isolated blocks of Jurassic carbonates in a highly deformed Triassic evaporite sequence. The single site in the Prebetic has not rotated significantly relative to stable Iberia. Introduction The Betic-Rif arc of southern Spain and northern Morocco is a Late Cretaceous to Neo- gene mountain chain related to convergence be- tween Africa and Eurasia. During the Neogene the older, dominantly metamorphic Internal Zones underwent extensional collapse, forming the Alboran Sea between Spain and Morocco and driving compressional deformation in the external fold and thrust belt [1]. The External Zones of the Betic Cordillera in Sp

ere measured, in Ox- ford, on a CCL cryogenic magnetometer. Stan- dard measurement procedure involved stepwise thermal magnetisation until no measurable signal could be identified (typically ~ 0.02 mA/m, or less than 2% of the initial intensity). Initially, bulk susceptibility was measured after each de- magnetisation step to monitor growth of magnetic minerals during heating, but where no significant change was noted this was discontinued. Compo- nents were analysed on orthogonal plots using a least-squares routine. IRM acquisition and de- magnetisation experiments were completed on one sample from each site to investigate the magnetic mineralogy. 3. The rotations occurred after latest Oligocene times, and probably before the late Miocene. This overlaps a period of dextrally oblique convergence during the early to middle Miocene along the Internal/External Zone Boundary and within the External Zone. Rotations in the External Zone are recorded by palaeomagnetic results from 27 sites in Upper Jurassic (Ammonitico rosso facies) limestones from the Subbetic Zone, and one site of a similar age from the Prebetic. The sites show either two- or three-component behaviour. The low-temperature component is coincident with the present-field direction. The intermediate-temperature component was probably acquired during Miocene folding. The high-temperature component passes fold tests (Miocene age) and a conglomerate test (Eocene-early Oligocene age). Palaeomagnetic declinations from individual tectonic blocks in the Subbetic are consistent, but indicate large differential rotations between blocks. These blocks

dent with the present-field direction. The intermediate-temperature component was probably acquired during Miocene folding. The high-temperature component passes fold tests (Miocene age) and a conglomerate test (Eocene-early Oligocene age). Palaeomagnetic declinations from individual tectonic blocks in the Subbetic are consistent, but indicate large differential rotations between blocks. These blocks are underlain by low-angle thrust faults, which probably accommodated much of the rotation. The largest rotations occur on relatively small isolated blocks of Jurassic carbonates in a highly deformed Triassic evaporite sequence. The single site in the Prebetic has not rotated significantly relative to stable Iberia. In Malaguide rocks of the Sierra Espufia, in the adjacent Internal Zone, stable palaeomagnetic components were measured at one site in upper Miocene sedimentary rocks, at three sites in upper Oligocene-lower Miocene red marls, at one site in Oligocene marls, at one site in Jurassic limestones, and at two sites in Permo-Triassic red beds. The palaeomagnetic results suggest that about 60 ° of clockwise rotation occurred in the latest Oligocene-earliest Miocene, and a further 140 ° of clockwise rotation subsequently. In Malaguide rocks of the Sierra Espufia, in the adjacent Internal Zone, stable palaeomagnetic components were measured at one site in upper Miocene sedimentary rocks, at three sites in upper Oligocene-lower Miocene red marls, at one site in Oligocene marls, at one site in Jurassic limestones, and at two sites in Permo-Triassic red beds. The palaeomagnetic results suggest that about 60 ° of clockwise rotation occurred in the latest Oligocene-earliest Miocene, and a further 140 ° of clockwise rotation subsequently. One site in late Miocene sedimentary rocks yields unrotated declinations which, if not representing an overprinted direction, indicate that the rotation was complete by the end of the Miocene. 1. Introduction The Betic-Rif arc of southern Spain and northern Morocco is a Late Cretaceous to Neo- gene mountain chain related to convergence be- tween Africa and Eurasia. During the Neogene the older, dominantly metamorphic Internal Zones underwent extensional collapse, forming the Alboran Sea between Spain and Morocco and driving compressional deformation in the external fold and thrust belt [1]. The External Zones of the Betic Cordillera in Sp

ntact, separating the Iberian margin from the Alboran microplate. Recent palaeomagnetic studies in the Subbetic Zone have demonstrated a consistent pattern of clockwise rotations about vertical axes [9,10]. 0012-821X/93/$06.00 © 1993 - Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. All rights reserved 226 S. ALLIERTON ET AL. These rotations confirm that there has been a component of dextral shear in the deformation, and Osete et al. [9] suggest that the rotational deformation occurred by distributed simple shear, either during Miocene oblique convergence, or during late Miocene-Recent deformation. The purpose of this paper is to present the palaeomagnetic results of a detailed programme of investigation in the eastern Betic Cordillera, with the aim of determining the relationship be- tween the vertical-axis rotations and the regional tectonics. In the first part we address the varia- tion in rotational deformation across part of the External Zone, and its spatial relationship to thrusts and strike-slip faults, and in the second part we present evidence for the timing of rota- tion from unmetamorphosed sediments of the structurally highest tectonic unit of the Internal Zone (the Malaguide Complex). 2. Progressive thermal demagnetization isolated single characteristic component magnetizations in the limestone unit and two components in the sandstones; all components show mixed polarities. The mean direction in the limestone unit is 352/- 34 (in-situ) and 1/- 4 (tilt-corrected) (a95 = 12°). Component 1 in the sandstones isolated within higher temperature ranges exhibits consistent directions in five sites out of six, yielding an overall site mean direction of 36/75, k = 10, a95 = 45 (in-situ) and 355/13, k = 178, ol95 = 5.2 (tilt-corrected) and passes a fold test at the 99% confidence level. The directions of component 2 with lower unblocking temperatures in the sandstones are best grouped at 10% unfolding (k = 278, a95 = 6), giving a mean direction of 351/18 that conforms to the mean directions of the characteristic component in the limestone unit as well as component 1 in the first five sandstone sites. Our interpretation, therefore, is that all the magnetizations in the both limestones and the sandstones were acquired at the time of folding. Our paleomagnetic directions from Guizhou are similar to those of Paleozoic rocks, from which folding associated remagnetiza- tions were also observed, in the vicinity of Nanjing in the northeastern part of the Yangtze Block. The folding associated remagnetizations in both areas thus most likely have the same age, i.e., Late Triassic/Jurassic. We further infer that the southern Guizhou province has not been rotated since Late Triassic/Jurassic times by considering the similarity of the pole positions obtained from remagnetizations in Yunnan, Guizhou and the Nanjing area. Moreover, we suggest a new early Mesozoic apparent polar wander loop for the South China Block, going through the poles of the Triassic/Jurassic remagnetizations. This loop points to rotations of the South China Block as a whole during the late Triassic-Jurassic period. I. Introduction Asia is a composite continent formed by the accretion, mainly during Phanerozoic times, of various crustal blocks [1,2]. The geographical en- tity of China is composed of several relatively stable cratons, such as Tarim, Sino-Korea and Yangtze, apparently welded and bounded by mo- bile fold belts [3]. South China consists of at least two ancient tectonic units, i.e., the Yangtze cra- ton or paraplatform that has

he- ory, do not explain the coherent poles from Nan- jing, southern Guizhou and eastern Yunnan (Fig. 8). This coherence suggests a rotation of south China as a whole, i.e., apparent polar wander. This means that a new loop must be included in the Apparent Polar Wander Path for South China, going through the poles calculated from the fold- ing-associated remagnetization results obtained in the Nanjing area and the southern Guizhou and eastern Yunnan provinces (Fig. 8). The age of this loop is, as argued above, constrained to the late Triassic/Jurassic interval. The modification that is made herein for the Mesozoic segment of the APWP for South China is preliminary. More compelling evidence for the loop will certainly depend on the acquisition of more Mesozoic paleomagnetic data. Its age cali- bration will depend, moreover, on more precise dating of the folding phases that deformed the rocks involved in our studies. from 14 sites were collected, including sandstone samples from two limbs of a fold. Progressive thermal demagnetization isolated single characteristic component magnetizations in the limestone unit and two components in the sandstones; all components show mixed polarities. The mean direction in the limestone unit is 352/- 34 (in-situ) and 1/- 4 (tilt-corrected) (a95 = 12°). Component 1 in the sandstones isolated within higher temperature ranges exhibits consistent directions in five sites out of six, yielding an overall site mean direction of 36/75, k = 10, a95 = 45 (in-situ) and 355/13, k = 178, ol95 = 5.2 (tilt-corrected) and passes a fold test at the 99% confidence level. The directions of component 2 with lower unblocking temperatures in the sandstones are best grouped at 10% unfolding (k = 278, a95 = 6), giving a mean direction of 351/18 that conforms to the mean directions of the characteristic component in the limestone unit as well as component 1 in the first five sandstone sites. Our interpretation, therefore, is that all the magnetizations in the both limestones and the sandstones were acquired at the time of folding. Our paleomagnetic directions from Guizhou are similar to those of Paleozoic rocks, from which folding associated remagnetiza- tions were also observed,

at the time of folding. Our paleomagnetic directions from Guizhou are similar to those of Paleozoic rocks, from which folding associated remagnetiza- tions were also observed, in the vicinity of Nanjing in the northeastern part of the Yangtze Block. The folding associated remagnetizations in both areas thus most likely have the same age, i.e., Late Triassic/Jurassic. We further infer that the southern Guizhou province has not been rotated since Late Triassic/Jurassic times by considering the similarity of the pole positions obtained from remagnetizations in Yunnan, Guizhou and the Nanjing area. Moreover, we suggest a new early Mesozoic apparent polar wander loop for the South China Block, going through the poles of the Triassic/Jurassic remagnetizations. This loop points to rotations of the South China Block as a whole during the late Triassic-Jurassic period. I. Introduction Asia is a composite continent formed by the accretion, mainly during Phanerozoic times, of various crustal blocks [1,2]. The geographical en- tity of China is composed of several relatively stable cratons, such as Tarim, Sino-Korea and Yangtze, apparently welded and bounded by mo- bile fold belts [3]. South China consists of at least two ancient tectonic units, i.e., the Yangtze cra- ton or paraplatform that has

he- ory, do not explain the coherent poles from Nan- jing, southern Guizhou and eastern Yunnan (Fig. 8). This coherence suggests a rotation of south China as a whole, i.e., apparent polar wander. This means that a new loop must be included in the Apparent Polar Wander Path for South China, going through the poles calculated from the fold- ing-associated remagnetization results obtained in the Nanjing area and the southern Guizhou and eastern Yunnan provinces (Fig. 8). The age of this loop is, as argued above, constrained to the late Triassic/Jurassic interval. The modification that is made herein for the Mesozoic segment of the APWP for South China is preliminary. More compelling evidence for the loop will certainly depend on the acquisition of more Mesozoic paleomagnetic data. Its age cali- bration will depend, moreover, on more precise dating of the folding phases that deformed the rocks involved in our studies. from 14 sites were collected, including sandstone samples from two limbs of a fold. Progressive thermal demagnetization isolated single characteristic component magnetizations in the limestone unit and two components in the sandstones; all components show mixed polarities. The mean direction in the limestone unit is 352/- 34 (in-situ) and 1/- 4 (tilt-corrected) (a95 = 12°). Component 1 in the sandstones isolated within higher temperature ranges exhibits consistent directions in five sites out of six, yielding an overall site mean direction of 36/75, k = 10, a95 = 45 (in-situ) and 355/13, k = 178, ol95 = 5.2 (tilt-corrected) and passes a fold test at the 99% confidence level. The directions of component 2 with lower unblocking temperatures in the sandstones are best grouped at 10% unfolding (k = 278, a95 = 6), giving a mean direction of 351/18 that conforms to the mean directions of the characteristic component in the limestone unit as well as component 1 in the first five sandstone sites. Our interpretation, therefore, is that all the magnetizations in the both limestones and the sandstones were acquired at the time of folding. Our paleomagnetic directions from Guizhou are similar to those of Paleozoic rocks, from which folding associated remagnetiza- tions were also observed, in the vicinity of Nanjing in the northeastern part of the Yangtze Block. The folding associated remagnetizations in both areas thus most likely have the same age, i.e., Late Triassic/Jurassic. We further infer that the southern Guizhou province has not been rotated since Late Triassic/Jurassic times by considering the similarity of the pole positions obtained from remagnetizations in Yunnan, Guizhou and the Nanjing area. Moreover, we suggest a new early Mesozoic apparent polar wander loop for the South China Block, going through the poles of the Triassic/Jurassic remagnetizations. This loop points to rotations of the South China Block as a whole during the late Triassic-Jurassic period. I. The geographical en- tity of China is composed of several relatively stable cratons, such as Tarim, Sino-Korea and Yangtze, apparently welded and bounded by mo- bile fold belts [3]. Three of these poles are also plotted, after rotation in European coordinates (ornament 4, Fig. 11: N1, Newark Supergroup volcanics [45]; N2, Newark Basin overprint [46]; Mvr, Moat vol- canics reversed overprint [38]). This seems to support the reality of a higher latitude track in Jurassic time, although considering the associated errors this is not conclusive. Nevertheless, in this framework the Kerforne pole (ornament 3, Fig. 11) seems to be the first indication of the exis- tence of a cusp around 200 Ma in the European APWP. d October 27, 1992; revision accepted March 5, 1993 ABSTRACT A paleomagnetic study was carried out on 23 sites sampled in Paleocene, Eocene and Lower Miocene sedimentary formations of the Western Taurides belt east of the Isparta reentrant. The paleomagnetic data, based on twelve suitable sites, record a coherent post-Eocene ~ 40 ° clockwise rotation throughout the area studied. We interpret this regional rotation as a semi-rigid rotation of the whole Western Taurides belt above a major deep d4collement level. Together with previously published data, these new results suggest that the Isparta reentrant would result from diachronous opposite rotations of the two branches: first a late Eocene-Oligocene clockwise rotation of the Akseki-Beysehir Taurides initiating the Tauride arc, and then anticlockwise rotation of the Lycian Taurides, probably during Middle Miocene times. I. Introduction The Alpine Mediterranean belt constitutes a wide zone of continental collision made up of a succession of arcs. Many of these arcs surround extensional basins whereas a few others appear as deformed margins wrapping crustal blocks. In the Eastern Mediterranean, both of these types of structures are well illustrated by the Hellenic belt around the Aegean Sea and the Tauride belt around

In the Eastern Mediterranean, both of these types of structures are well illustrated by the Hellenic belt around the Aegean Sea and the Tauride belt around the Kirsehir block (Fig. 1). Paleomagnetic work conducted previously along the Aegean Arc, including on Lycian Tau- rides situated west of Isparta, has shown that its present-day curvature results from two successive rotational phases [1]. d October 27, 1992; revision accepted March 5, 1993 ABSTRACT A paleomagnetic study was carried out on 23 sites sampled in Paleocene, Eocene and Lower Miocene sedimentary formations of the Western Taurides belt east of the Isparta reentrant. The paleomagnetic data, based on twelve suitable sites, record a coherent post-Eocene ~ 40 ° clockwise rotation throughout the area studied. We interpret this regional rotation as a semi-rigid rotation of the whole Western Taurides belt above a major deep d4collement level. Together with previously published data, these new results suggest that the Isparta reentrant would result from diachronous opposite rotations of the two branches: first a late Eocene-Oligocene clockwise rotation of the Akseki-Beysehir Taurides initiating the Tauride arc, and then anticlockwise rotation of the Lycian Taurides, probably during Middle Miocene times. I. Introduction The Alpine Mediterranean belt constitutes a wide zone of continental collision made up of a succession of arcs. Many of these arcs surround extensional basins whereas a few others appear as deformed margins wrapping crustal blocks. In the Eastern Mediterranean, both of these types of structures are well illustrated by the Hellenic belt around the Aegean Sea and the Tauride belt around

In the Eastern Mediterranean, both of these types of structures are well illustrated by the Hellenic belt around the Aegean Sea and the Tauride belt around the Kirsehir block (Fig. 1). Paleomagnetic work conducted previously along the Aegean Arc, including on Lycian Tau- rides situated west of Isparta, has shown that its present-day curvature results from two successive rotational phases [1]. The tilt- corrected mean paleomagnetic direction of the twelve sites is D = 42.0 °, I= 51.1 °, with a95 = 15.7 °. The precision parameter k increases from 2.7 to 8.7 after tilt correction for the twelve sites. The remaining four sites (22, 29, 34 and 37) form the other group (group B). Their site mean directions reveal a divergence from the uncor- rected mean direction during tilt correction (Fig. 3 (2-B)). All four sites reveal normal polarity and their mean direction is similar to the present geomagnetic field (D = 7.8 °, I= 45.9 °) in situ. The precision parameter decreases from 16.1 to 5.0 after tilt correction. The rocks of this group probably acquired their magnetization after tilt- ing occurred. 4. Discussion 4.1 Characteristic direction of the Jingxing Forma- tion Our paleomagnetic study indicates that the twelve group A sites acquired their stable magne- tization before folding, whereas the remaining four sites (group B) acquired their magnetization after folding. The group A sites probably pre- serve the reliable paleomagnetic direction of the Lower Cretaceous Jingxing Formation. These twelve group A sites provide a positive fold test which is significant at 99% confidence level [15]. We recognize here that the directions of site 8, 20 and 21 are of reversed polarity because of their negative inclination value. The mean of the group A sites (D = 42.0 °, I= 51.1 °, with a95 = 15.7°; Fig. 3(3)) probably represents the characteristic formation mean of the Jingxing Formation. The dispersion of the declinations in the pale- omagnetic directions of the group A sites appears to be larger than that of the inclinations (see Fig. 3 (3)). We therefore ex- clude the paleomagnetic results of the secondar- ily magnetized group from the characteristic di- rections of the Jinxing Formation. 4.2 Easterly paleomagnetic direction of the Jingx- ing Formation A large clockwise deflection in declination (D = 42 °) appears in the paleomagnetic directions of the Lower Cretaceous rocks of the Yongping area. The reliability of the easterly direction is ascertained through the presence of normal and reversed polarities and through thermal demag- netization and the fold test. The reversed direc- tion of site 21 is reasonably antipodal to the normal ones. Although site 8 and 9 are far re- moved from the mean direction, they are antipo- dal each other. The positive fold test demon- strates this easterly direction as a prefolding one. Because the folding in the study area probably took place in the Paleogene [10,20], the prefold- ing magnetization is probably the Cretaceous pa- leomagnetic direction. Our current research concerns the rever- sals records (from the lower Thvera to the Gauss/Matuyama boundary) which are located in the Rossello composite section. This section consists of the marine marls from the Trubi and the Narbone Formation [4,5]. NRS 1093), Universit~ Paris VII, 4place Jussieu, 75252 Paris Cedex 05, France Received January 6, 1993; revision accepted January 29, 1993 ABSTRACT We present the magnetostratigraphy of the late Triassic pelagic Kavur Tepe section from the Taurides southwestern Turkey). The section investigated is about 30 m thick and consists of fine-grained whitish limestones. The biostratigraphy, based on the conodont zonation, gives an age from the Lacian 2 zone (lower Norian) to the Sevatian 2 zone (upper Norian). The paleomagnetic analyses indicate very favourable behaviour, with two magnetic components which can be isolated both by thermal and AF demagnetization. The magnetization is carried by magnetite and goethite, which are clearly evident in IRM experiments. The first component of normal magnetic polarity has roughly the direction of the present-day field. The high unblocking temperature component shows directions of both polarities. In total, fifteen magnetic polarity intervals are observed within the Kavur Tepe section. The characteristic calculated Fisherian mean direction is particularly tightly grouped: D = 220.2 ° and I = 32.1 °, with K = 40.9, a95 = 1.7 ° and Nsamp = 179 (after bedding correction). cularly nu- merous, covering nearly all the terranes that con- stitute Tibet and the surrounding regions. This allows us to compare the results from South ~ind Southwest Yunnan with those from Tibet and its neighboring areas. These data are summarized in Table 3 and presented in Fig. 8 in terms of paleomagnetic rotation and latitude difference. Because our attention is focused on the effect of the India-Asia collision on the deformation of the Asian continent, results from the area south of the Indus-Zangbo Suture [e.g., 27] are not included. The selected data were obtained by employing magnetic cleaning techniques (prim- arily thermal demagnetization) and were calcu- lated on site means (with the exception of the mean paleomagnetic directions from the Pamir- Punjab Syntaxis, which were calculated at the sample level [28,29]). Early acquisition of the magnetization in most studies was established with a positive fold test and dual polarity. n accepted March 31, 1993 ABSTRACT Cretaceous and Jurassic redbeds have been sampled from South and Southwest Yunnan, China, for paleomagnetic study. The paleomagnetic directions resolved from the Cretaceous rocks indicate that the Xiaguan area, which is located on the Red River fault, has not been rotated with respect to stable Eurasia since at least Late Cretaceous times and that the Jinggu-Mengla area 200-400 km farther south has been rotated by 46-65 ° clockwise. The Jurassic results reveal the same rotation pattern. At face value, the differences between the observed Cretaceous paleolatitudes and those predicted from the Eurasian apparent polar wander path (APWP) indicate a southward extrusion of the region, but the amount of extrusion is not large enough to be resolved by paleomagnetic methods. Comparison with Mesozoic paleomagnetic data from central Yunnan, northern Thailand and northwestern Borneo suggests that the Red River fault is not a demarcation between unrotated and significantly rotated regions, and that Sundaland did not respond to the India-Asia collision as a single coherent unit. The good internal consistency and striking deviation from the present field of the ChRM of the Hepingxiang Formation suggest its non-recent origin. More interestingly, the pale- opole determined from the B component is coin- cident with that of the middle Cretaceous Man- gang Formation and the paleopole derived from the C component overlaps that of the Middle Jurassic Hepingxiang Formation (Fig. 7). This indicates that the B component of the Mengga Formation might be a Cretaceous overprint co- eval with the ChRM of the Mangang Formation, and that the C component of the Mengga Forma- tion and the ChRM of the Hepingxiang Forma- tion might have been acquired during Jurassic times. Finally, the mean direction for the Upper Jurassic Bazhulu Formation is based upon only five sites from a monoclinal section, and needs to be confirmed by future study. The fact that the inclination is gentler than that of the present-day field in geographic coordinates and the grouping of the site mean directions is improved after tilt correction, however, suggests that the ChRM of the Bazhulu Formation is probably not a recent overprint.

The molasse deposits of Eocene- Pliocene age unconformably overlie the redbed sequence. In the Simao Depression, the total thickness of the Jurassic-Cretaceous sequence is over 6000 m [12]. The Jurassic succession is composed of three formations, from bottom to top the Lower Juras- sic Yangjiang Formation, the Middle Jurassic Hepingxiang (in the western part of the depres- sion) or Huakaizuo (in the eastern part) Forma- tion, and the Upper Jurassic Bazhulu Formation [13,14]. The age of these rocks is primarily controlled by such fauna as bivalves, gastropods and ostrapods [14- 16]. The Middle Jurassic Hepingxiang/Huakaizuo Formation and the Lower Cretaceous Jingxing Formation are especially useful in correlating and mapping this thick redbed sequence due to their variegated color and rich fossil content. The molasse deposits of Eocene- Pliocene age unconformably overlie the redbed sequence. In the Simao Depression, the total thickness of the Jurassic-Cretaceous sequence is over 6000 m [12]. The Jurassic succession is composed of three formations, from bottom to top the Lower Juras- sic Yangjiang Formation, the Middle Jurassic Hepingxiang (in the western part of the depres- sion) or Huakaizuo (in the eastern part) Forma- tion, and the Upper Jurassic Bazhulu Formation [13,14]. The overlying Cretaceous sequence is also divided into three parts [15]: the Lower Creta- ceous is designated as the Jingxing Formation, the middle Cretaceous includes the Mangang and Pashahe formations, and the Upper Cretaceous is represented by the Mankuanhe Formation. The age of these rocks is primarily controlled by such fauna as bivalves, gastropods and ostrapods [14- 16]. The Middle Jurassic Hepingxiang/Huakaizuo Formation and the Lower Cretaceous Jingxing Formation are especially useful in correlating and mapping this thick redbed sequence due to their variegated color and rich fossil content. Conclusions (1) RLR, the characteristic magnetization of the unaltered Red Lake batholiths, is probably a primary TRM acquired ~ 2700 Ma ago (4°Ar/ 39Ar initial cooling age [3]) and carried by both magnetite and deuteric hematite. Evidence for a primary TRM origin includes its generally high unblocking temperatures (> 550°C), coercivities (> 40 mT), and NRM intensities (> 100 mA/m), as well as the pristine condition of the visible silicate and opaque minerals in thin section. (2) RLG, the characteristic magnetization of sheared, altered and metamorphosed units in and near the deformation zones (DZs), is a secondary CRM or TCRM ~ 2580 Ma old. n, North Island, New Zealand, contains a complex sedimentary record of Lower and Middle Pleistocene sea-level changes. Palaeomagnetic results allow identification of the Matuyama/Brunhes transition, the Jaramillo Subehron and the Cobb Mountain Subchron. Correlations of rhyolitic tuff horizons across the basin are consistent with magnetostratigraphic correlations between sections. Isothermal plateau fission-track (ITPFT) ages of 1.05 _+ 0.05 Ma and 1.63 _+ 0.15 Ma on two tufts (Potaka Pumice and Pakihikura Pumice, respectively) are consistent with the interpreted magnetostratigraphy and also with the astronomically tuned timescale of ODP Site 677. Magnetostratigraphy and ITPFT ages allow correlation of sedimentary cycles at Wanganui with odd-numbered oxygen isotope stages 17-31 in deep-sea cores. The stratotype section for the New Zealand Castlecliffian Stage is shown to be incomplete relative to other studied sections in the basin. Below stage 31, the character of the cyclothems changes at Wanganui, from marine dominated, to a greater representation of non-marine and estuarine strata. This change may be partly related to a change in amplitude and frequency of climatic cycles identified in oxygen isotope records, but the primary cause is likely to be increased basinal uplif

nsed shellbed, rich in offshore molluscan fos- sils, that is succeeded by a sparsely fossiliferous shelf siltstone which is usually truncated by the basal unconformity of the overlying sequence. The mid-cycle shellbed is therefore interpreted to be broadly equivalent to the maximum flooding sur- face of a sea-level cycle. Massive siltstones at the tops of cycles are interpreted as having been deposited during the sea-level high stand and, in some cases, part of the shoaling upwards cycle is preserved [14]. The sequence-bounding uncon- formities represent surfaces of marine planation cut by the landward passage of the shoreface of the transgressing sea. Mi- cropegmatitic intergrowths of quartzofeldspathic material occasionally occur along some plagio- clase grain boundaries in both gabbro and do- lerite. In the leucogabbro, slight deuteric alter- ation of clinopyroxene into pale green amphibole (actinolite) is common along internal cleavages and grain boundaries. However, the amphibole does not occur as independent grains or entirely replace original minerals. Fe-Ti oxides occur as dispersed grains, locally with skeletal shapes. ampled for palaeomagnetic investigation across the total geo- graphic distribution of central Kerala dyke swarms. These included eight sites within NW-SE trending dolerites and three within the NNW- SSE trending leucogabbro dyke. At each site at least six oriented block samples were collected within an individual dyke, using a magnetic com- pass for orientation. ke swarms occurring within the granulite terrain in central Kerala (west coast of India). Palaeomagnetic data show that the NNW-SSE leucogabbro dykes sampled are normally magnetised (D = 307 and I = -57), whereas most NW-SE dolerite dykes are reversely magnetised (D = 163 and I = 61). One dolerite dyke shows normal polarity. The present 4°Ar/39Ar isotope ages for dolerite dykes and previously reported K-Ar ages for leucogabbros suggest 81 + 2 Ma for acquisition of the leucogabbro directions and 69 + 1 Ma for acquisition of the reverse magnetic directions within the dolerites. Based on palaeomagnetic and isotopic age data, the dolerite dykes appears to represent feeder systems for the Deccan volcanic sequences. We suggest that the Deccan eruptions were widespread, and probably extended southward at least into central Kerala. The leucogabbros may correspond to the 34N superchron and represent a plume-related magmatic episode precursory to the main volcanic event. These data suggest that an early intraplate plume tectonic setting (since ca. 80 Ma) preceded lithospheric thinning, asthenospheric upwelling and consequent massive flood volcanism during the period 70-65 Ma. This culminated in ocean-floor spreading between the Seychelles-Mascarene and continental India. I. Introduction Several Phanerozoic dyke swarms are exposed along the west coast of southern India. Similarly, although many conventional K-Ar iso- tope ages have been reported for Deccan rocks, the duration of Deccan volcanism has been un- certain [1], and relationships between the dykes and Deccan volcanism have not been properly evaluated. The gabbro dyke is aligned to nearly linear, with only limited offsets along a total strike length of > 100 km. The dolerite dykes vary in length and can reach ca. 10 km, and they parallel each other within a zone that is ca. > 50 km wide. The gabbro dyke is relatively thick (20-50 m), whereas the dolerites are thin, with maximum widths of ca. < 5 m. The dolerites locally crosscut the NNW-SSE trending leucogabbro dyke, proving that the former are younger. The contacts of both dyke systems are sharp, with well-developed chilled margins and steep dips. 3. Petrographic and geochemical characteristics The petrological and geochemical characteris- tics of the studied dykes have been discussed in detail elsewhere [6]. Both the dolerites and the gabbro consist dominantly of plagioclase, clinopy- roxene and opaque minerals. The dolerites locally contain minor olivine. Apatite is a common ac- cessory mineral and quartz occurs frequently as an interstitial constituent in the gabbro. Plagio- clase occurs locally as phenocrysts or as glomero- crysts in an ophitic matrix of plagioclase and pyroxene in the dolerites. In the gabbro the pla- gioclase is equigranular and clinopyroxene com- monly occurs as

y as phenocrysts or as glomero- crysts in an ophitic matrix of plagioclase and pyroxene in the dolerites. In the gabbro the pla- gioclase is equigranular and clinopyroxene com- monly occurs as an interstitial constituent. Mi- cropegmatitic intergrowths of quartzofeldspathic material occasionally occur along some plagio- clase grain boundaries in both gabbro and do- lerite. In the leucogabbro, slight deuteric alter- ation of clinopyroxene into pale green amphibole (actinolite) is common along internal cleavages and grain boundaries. However, the amphibole does not occur as independent grains or entirely replace original minerals. Fe-Ti oxides occur as dispersed grains, locally with skeletal shapes. Geochemical characteristics suggest that the dolerites and the gabbro were derived from dis- crete parental magmas [6]. In terms of incompati- ble trace elements, the dolerites are correlative with tholeiitic units within upper stratigraphic units in the Deccan basalts. The gabbros show general geochemical correlations with alkaline- type rocks exposed in northern parts of the Dec- can province [6]. 216 Z Radhakrishna et al. /Earth and Planetary Science Letters 121 (1994) 213-226 4. ampled for palaeomagnetic investigation across the total geo- graphic distribution of central Kerala dyke swarms. These included eight sites within NW-SE trending dolerites and three within the NNW- SSE trending leucogabbro dyke. At each site at least six oriented block samples were collected within an individual dyke, using a magnetic com- pass for orientation. These were later set in the laboratory to obtain oriented cylindrical speci- mens (1" × 1") for laboratory measurements. A Molspin Minispin spinner magnetometer (UK) was used for remanent vector measure- ments. Specimens were treated by both alternat- ing field (AF) and thermal demagnetisation tech- niques using a Moispinn AC shielded demagne- riser and an MMTD-1 thermal demagnetiser (Magnetic Measurements, UK) in a field-free space. AC demagnetisations were performed in progressive steps at close intervals (2.5 mT) and thermal demagnetisations on specimens repre- sentative of each site up to > 600°C in steps of 50°C. ke swarms occurring within the granulite terrain in central Kerala (west coast of India). Palaeomagnetic data show that the NNW-SSE leucogabbro dykes sampled are normally magnetised (D = 307 and I = -57), whereas most NW-SE dolerite dykes are reversely magnetised (D = 163 and I = 61). One dolerite dyke shows normal polarity. The present 4°Ar/39Ar isotope ages for dolerite dykes and previously reported K-Ar ages for leucogabbros suggest 81 + 2 Ma for acquisition of the leucogabbro directions and 69 + 1 Ma for acquisition of the reverse magnetic directions within the dolerites. Based on palaeomagnetic and isotopic age data, the dolerite dykes appears to represent feeder systems for the Deccan volcanic sequences. We suggest that the Deccan eruptions were widespread, and probably extended southward at least into central Kerala. The entire magmatic episode may have occurred between ca. 70 and 65 Ma (during the 31R period probably corresponding to the Cretaceous/Tertiary boundary). The leucogabbros may correspond to the 34N superchron and represent a plume-related magmatic episode precursory to the main volcanic event. The leucogabbros may correspond to the 34N superchron and represent a plume-related magmatic episode precursory to the main volcanic event. These data suggest that an early intraplate plume tectonic setting (since ca. 80 Ma) preceded lithospheric thinning, asthenospheric upwelling and consequent massive flood volcanism during the period 70-65 Ma. This culminated in ocean-floor spreading between the Seychelles-Mascarene and continental India. I. Introduction Several Phanerozoic dyke swarms are exposed along the west coast of southern India. These have generally been considered to be related to the Deccan basalts. However, neither reliable palaeomagnetic directions nor precise radiomet- [uc] ric ages have been available for these dykes. Similarly, although many conventional K-Ar iso- tope ages have been reported for Deccan rocks, the duration of Deccan volcanism has been un- certain [1], and relationships between the dykes and Deccan volcanism have not been properly evaluated. Paleomagnetism In the laboratory, individual specimens 25 mm in diameter and 23 mm long were prepared from the samples. Characteristic directions with a high unblocking temperature component above 560°C are isolated from 24 sites. Westerly declinations (D = - 1 ° ~ - 91 °) are identified in welded tufts older than 17 Ma from these areas. When combined with previous paleomagnetic data from welded tufts, the Early Miocene paleomagnetic poles derived from northeast Honshu Island and the Oshima Peninsula are statisti- cally identical and indicate that northeast Honshu Island and the Oshima Peninsula were subjected to counterclock- wise rotation as a sin

rotating block of Northeast Japan extends north to the Oshima Peninsula to the latitude 43°N. The dimension of this rotating block is of the order of 500 kin. The paleomagnetic data provide a best curve for the rotation process, with the counterclockwise rotation reaching a climax at 15.0 Ma and a net amount of rotation of 46.4 °. The 500 km long Northeast Japan block was rotated counterclockwise through more than 45 ° and accompanied a clockwise rotation of the 600 km long Southwest Japan block at about 15 Ma. 1. Introduction Peripheral parts of the continental crust typi- cally behave as a non-rigid assemblage associated with the formation of back-arc basins. As a con- sequence continental material is often split into blocks which separate from the mother continent [1]. A typical example is observed in the Japan arc and Sea of Japan system (Fig. 1). From the [UCl evidence of recent paleomagnetic studies along the Japan arc and ODP results from the Japan Sea [2-6], continental blocks forming the Japan arc are interpreted to have drifted and rotated as a consequence of the opening of the Sea of Japan between 25 and 12 Ma. A number of models have been proposed for the rifting process on the basis of geological and geophysical data derived from the Sea of Japan area

The regional extent of the rigid block compris- ing SW Japan during this clockwise rotational motion has been clearly established. Itoh and Ito [8] show from paleomagnetic evidence that the area from Kyushu to Fukui behaved as an intact block during the rotation. The le

geological observations suggest that the rigid area of NE Japan ranges from the Kanto district to the west- ern part of Hokkaido Island (see Fig. 1 and [1,9-12]), most paleomagnetic studies have sug- gested that only northeast Honshu Island was rotated counterclockwise as an intact block [2,13- 15]. Kawai et al. [15] note the possibility of rela- tive rotation between the western part of Hokkaido Island and northeast Honshu Island. These controversies relate to the lack of paleo- magnetic data from the northern part of Honshu Island and the western part of Hokkaido Island. As a step toward resolving this issue we have collected samples from the Yamagata area on Honshu Island to the western part of Hokkaido Island (Fig. 1). The primary subject of our paleo- magnetic study is the Oligocene to Late Miocene welded tuffs. These are highlighted because the rotational motion of NE Japan occurred during this period [2,14,16] and because welded tuffs have been shown to provide reliable magnetiza- tions and radiometric ages. 2. Characteristic directions with a high unblocking temperature component above 560°C are isolated from 24 sites. Westerly declinations (D = - 1 ° ~ - 91 °) are identified in welded tufts older than 17 Ma from these areas. When combined with previous paleomagnetic data from welded tufts, the Early Miocene paleomagnetic poles derived from northeast Honshu Island and the Oshima Peninsula are statisti- cally identical and indicate that northeast Honshu Island and the Oshima Peninsula were subjected to counterclock- wise rotation as a sin

rotating block of Northeast Japan extends north to the Oshima Peninsula to the latitude 43°N. The dimension of this rotating block is of the order of 500 kin. The paleomagnetic data provide a best curve for the rotation process, with the counterclockwise rotation reaching a climax at 15.0 Ma and a net amount of rotation of 46.4 °. The 500 km long Northeast Japan block was rotated counterclockwise through more than 45 ° and accompanied a clockwise rotation of the 600 km long Southwest Japan block at about 15 Ma. 1. Introduction Peripheral parts of the continental crust typi- cally behave as a non-rigid assemblage associated with the formation of back-arc basins. As a con- sequence continental material is often split into blocks which separate from the mother continent [1]. A typical example is observed in the Japan arc and Sea of Japan system (Fig. 1). From the [UCl evidence of recent paleomagnetic studies along the Japan arc and ODP results from the Japan Sea [2-6], continental blocks forming the Japan arc are interpreted to have drifted and rotated as a consequence of the opening of the Sea of Japan between 25 and 12 Ma. A number of models have been proposed for the rifting process on the basis of geological and geophysical data derived from the Sea of Japan area

The regional extent of the rigid block compris- ing SW Japan during this clockwise rotational motion has been clearly established. Itoh and Ito [8] show from paleomagnetic evidence that the area from Kyushu to Fukui behaved as an intact block during the rotation. The le

geological observations suggest that the rigid area of NE Japan ranges from the Kanto district to the west- ern part of Hokkaido Island (see Fig. 1 and [1,9-12]), most paleomagnetic studies have sug- gested that only northeast Honshu Island was rotated counterclockwise as an intact block [2,13- 15]. Kawai et al. [15] note the possibility of rela- tive rotation between the western part of Hokkaido Island and northeast Honshu Island. These controversies relate to the lack of paleo- magnetic data from the northern part of Honshu Island and the western part of Hokkaido Island. As a step toward resolving this issue we have collected samples from the Yamagata area on Honshu Island to the western part of Hokkaido Island (Fig. 1). The primary subject of our paleo- magnetic study is the Oligocene to Late Miocene welded tuffs. These are highlighted because the rotational motion of NE Japan occurred during this period [2,14,16] and because welded tuffs have been shown to provide reliable magnetiza- tions and radiometric ages. 2. section_candidates.excerpt: ELSEVIER Earth and Planetary Science Letters 121 (1994) 503-518 EPSL Counterclockwise rotation of Northeast Japan: Paleomagnetic evidence for regional extent and timing of rotation Yo-ichiro Otofuji a, Ayumi Kambara a, Takaaki Matsuda b, Susumu Nohda ¢ a Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Faculty of Science, Kobe University, Kobe 657, Japan b Department of Geology, Faculty of Science, Himeji Institute of Technology, Himeji 671-22, Japan c Kyoto Sangyo University, Kamigamo, Kita-ku, Kyoto 603, Japan (Received August 19, 1993; revision accepted November 25, 1993) Abstract Early to Late Miocene welded tufts have been sampled from northeast Honshu Island and the Oshima Peninsula of Hokkaido Island, Japan for paleomagnetic study. Characteristic directions with a high unblocking temperature component above 560°C are isolated from 24 sites. Westerly declinations (D = - 1 ° ~ - 91 °) are identified in welded tufts older than 17 Ma from these areas. When combined with previous paleomagnetic data from welded tufts, the Early Miocene paleomagnetic poles derived from northeast Honshu Island and the Oshima Peninsula are statisti- cally identical and indicate that northeast Honshu Island and the Oshima Peninsula were subjected to counterclock- wise rotation as a sin

rotating block of Northeast Japan extends north to the Oshima Peninsula to the latitude 43°N. The dimension of this rotating block is of the order of 500 kin. The paleomagnetic data provide a best curve for the rotation process, with the counterclockwise rotation reaching a climax at 15.0 Ma and a net amount of rotation of 46.4 °. The 500 km long Northeast Japan block was rotated counterclockwise through more than 45 ° and accompanied a clockwise rotation of the 600 km long Southwest Japan block at about 15 Ma. 1. Introduction Peripheral parts of the continental crust typi- cally behave as a non-rigid assemblage associated with the formation of back-arc basins. As a con- sequence continental material is often split into blocks which separate from the mother continent [1]. A typical example is observed in the Japan arc and Sea of Japan system (Fig. 1). From the [UCl evidence of recent paleomagnetic studies along the Japan arc and ODP results from the Japan Sea [2-6], continental blocks forming the Japan arc are interpreted to have drifted and rotated as a consequence of the opening of the Sea of Japan between 25 and 12 Ma. A number of models have been proposed for the rifting process on the basis of geological and geophysical data derived from the Sea of Japan area

These two blocks are con- sidered to have experienced differential rotation when the Sea of Japan was opened. The regional extent of the rigid block compris- ing SW Japan during this clockwise rotational motion has been clearly established. Itoh and Ito [8] show from paleomagnetic evidence that the area from Kyushu to Fukui behaved as an intact block during the rotation. The le

geological observations suggest that the rigid area of NE Japan ranges from the Kanto district to the west- ern part of Hokkaido Island (see Fig. 1 and [1,9-12]), most paleomagnetic studies have sug- gested that only northeast Honshu Island was rotated counterclockwise as an intact block [2,13- 15]. Kawai et al. [15] note the possibility of rela- tive rotation between the western part of Hokkaido Island and northeast Honshu Island. These controversies relate to the lack of paleo- magnetic data from the northern part of Honshu Island and the western part of Hokkaido Island. As a step toward resolving this issue we have collected samples from the Yamagata area on Honshu Island to the western part of Hokkaido Island (Fig. 1). The primary subject of our paleo- magnetic study is the Oligocene to Late Miocene welded tuffs. These are highlighted because the rotational motion of NE Japan occurred during this period [2,14,16] and because welded tuffs have been shown to provide reliable magnetiza- tions and radiometric ages. 2. rotating block of Northeast Japan extends north to the Oshima Peninsula to the latitude 43°N. The dimension of this rotating block is of the order of 500 kin. The paleomagnetic data provide a best curve for the rotation process, with the counterclockwise rotation reaching a climax at 15.0 Ma and a net amount of rotation of 46.4 °. The 500 km long Northeast Japan block was rotated counterclockwise through more than 45 ° and accompanied a clockwise rotation of the 600 km long Southwest Japan block at about 15 Ma. 1. Introduction Peripheral parts of the continental crust typi- cally behave as a non-rigid assemblage associated with the formation of back-arc basins. As a con- sequence continental material is often split into blocks which separate from the mother continent [1]. A typical example is observed in the Japan arc and Sea of Japan system (Fig. 1). From the [UCl evidence of recent paleomagnetic studies along the Japan arc and ODP results from the Japan Sea [2-6], continental blocks forming the Japan arc are interpreted to have drifted and rotated as a consequence of the opening of the Sea of Japan between 25 and 12 Ma. A number of models have been proposed for the rifting process on the basis of geological and geophysical data derived from the Sea of Japan area

The regional extent of the rigid block compris- ing SW Japan during this clockwise rotational motion has been clearly established. Itoh and Ito [8] show from paleomagnetic evidence that the area from Kyushu to Fukui behaved as an intact block during the rotation. The le

geological observations suggest that the rigid area of NE Japan ranges from the Kanto district to the west- ern part of Hokkaido Island (see Fig. 1 and [1,9-12]), most paleomagnetic studies have sug- gested that only northeast Honshu Island was rotated counterclockwise as an intact block [2,13- 15]. Kawai et al. [15] note the possibility of rela- tive rotation between the western part of Hokkaido Island and northeast Honshu Island. These controversies relate to the lack of paleo- magnetic data from the northern part of Honshu Island and the western part of Hokkaido Island. As a step toward resolving this issue we have collected samples from the Yamagata area on Honshu Island to the western part of Hokkaido Island (Fig. 1). section_candidates.excerpt: ELSEVIER Earth and Planetary Science Letters 121 (1994) 503-518 EPSL Counterclockwise rotation of Northeast Japan: Paleomagnetic evidence for regional extent and timing of rotation Yo-ichiro Otofuji a, Ayumi Kambara a, Takaaki Matsuda b, Susumu Nohda ¢ a Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, Faculty of Science, Kobe University, Kobe 657, Japan b Department of Geology, Faculty of Science, Himeji Institute of Technology, Himeji 671-22, Japan c Kyoto Sangyo University, Kamigamo, Kita-ku, Kyoto 603, Japan (Received August 19, 1993; revision accepted November 25, 1993) Abstract Early to Late Miocene welded tufts have been sampled from northeast Honshu Island and the Oshima Peninsula of Hokkaido Island, Japan for paleomagnetic study. Characteristic directions with a high unblocking temperature component above 560°C are isolated from 24 sites. Westerly declinations (D = - 1 ° ~ - 91 °) are identified in welded tufts older than 17 Ma from these areas. When combined with previous paleomagnetic data from welded tufts, the Early Miocene paleomagnetic poles derived from northeast Honshu Island and the Oshima Peninsula are statisti- cally identical and indicate that northeast Honshu Island and the Oshima Peninsula were subjected to counterclock- wise rotation as a sin

rotating block of Northeast Japan extends north to the Oshima Peninsula to the latitude 43°N. The dimension of this rotating block is of the order of 500 kin. The paleomagnetic data provide a best curve for the rotation process, with the counterclockwise rotation reaching a climax at 15.0 Ma and a net amount of rotation of 46.4 °. The 500 km long Northeast Japan block was rotated counterclockwise through more than 45 ° and accompanied a clockwise rotation of the 600 km long Southwest Japan block at about 15 Ma. 1. Introduction Peripheral parts of the continental crust typi- cally behave as a non-rigid assemblage associated with the formation of back-arc basins. As a con- sequence continental material is often split into blocks which separate from the mother continent [1]. A typical example is observed in the Japan arc and Sea of Japan system (Fig. 1). From the [UCl evidence of recent paleomagnetic studies along the Japan arc and ODP results from the Japan Sea [2-6], continental blocks forming the Japan arc are interpreted to have drifted and rotated as a consequence of the opening of the Sea of Japan between 25 and 12 Ma. A number of models have been proposed for the rifting process on the basis of geological and geophysical data derived from the Sea of Japan area

These two blocks are con- sidered to have experienced differential rotation when the Sea of Japan was opened. The regional extent of the rigid block compris- ing SW Japan during this clockwise rotational motion has been clearly established. Itoh and Ito [8] show from paleomagnetic evidence that the area from Kyushu to Fukui behaved as an intact block during the rotation. The le

geological observations suggest that the rigid area of NE Japan ranges from the Kanto district to the west- ern part of Hokkaido Island (see Fig. 1 and [1,9-12]), most paleomagnetic studies have sug- gested that only northeast Honshu Island was rotated counterclockwise as an intact block [2,13- 15]. Kawai et al. [15] note the possibility of rela- tive rotation between the western part of Hokkaido Island and northeast Honshu Island. These controversies relate to the lack of paleo- magnetic data from the northern part of Honshu Island and the western part of Hokkaido Island. As a step toward resolving this issue we have collected samples from the Yamagata area on Honshu Island to the western part of Hokkaido Island (Fig. 1). The primary subject of our paleo- magnetic study is the Oligocene to Late Miocene welded tuffs. These are highlighted because the rotational motion of NE Japan occurred during this period [2,14,16] and because welded tuffs have been shown to provide reliable magnetiza- tions and radiometric ages. 2. Characteristic directions with a high unblocking temperature component above 560°C are isolated from 24 sites. Westerly declinations (D = - 1 ° ~ - 91 °) are identified in welded tufts older than 17 Ma from these areas. When combined with previous paleomagnetic data from welded tufts, the Early Miocene paleomagnetic poles derived from northeast Honshu Island and the Oshima Peninsula are statisti- cally identical and indicate that northeast Honshu Island and the Oshima Peninsula were subjected to counterclock- wise rotation as a sin

rotating block of Northeast Japan extends north to the Oshima Peninsula to the latitude 43°N. The dimension of this rotating block is of the order of 500 kin. The paleomagnetic data provide a best curve for the rotation process, with the counterclockwise rotation reaching a climax at 15.0 Ma and a net amount of rotation of 46.4 °. The 500 km long Northeast Japan block was rotated counterclockwise through more than 45 ° and accompanied a clockwise rotation of the 600 km long Southwest Japan block at about 15 Ma. 1. Introduction Peripheral parts of the continental crust typi- cally behave as a non-rigid assemblage associated with the formation of back-arc basins. As a con- sequence continental material is often split into blocks which separate from the mother continent [1]. A typical example is observed in the Japan arc and Sea of Japan system (Fig. 1). From the [UCl evidence of recent paleomagnetic studies along the Japan arc and ODP results from the Japan Sea [2-6], continental blocks forming the Japan arc are interpreted to have drifted and rotated as a consequence of the opening of the Sea of Japan between 25 and 12 Ma. A number of models have been proposed for the rifting process on the basis of geological and geophysical data derived from the Sea of Japan area

Kawai et al. [15] note the possibility of rela- tive rotation between the western part of Hokkaido Island and northeast Honshu Island. These units outcrop over a wide area in the western Southern Alps, although most of the sampled sections are in the vicinity of the Late Eocene-Early Oligocene Adamello batholith. Geological setting and sampling The Lesser Kuril Islands and the the Nemuro Peninsula in the easternmost part of Hokkaido are an area without present-day volcanic activity on the Pacific side of the Kuril island arc (Fig. 1). Upper Cretaceous volcanics, however, are com- mon in this area, and this is considered to repre- sent a remnant of a Late Cretaceous island arc which had originated on the oceanic crust, as is evident from the pyroxenite, gabbro and serpenti- nite xenoliths in Cretaceous basalts [8]. Upper Cretaceous rocks are found in two com- plexes, the upper complex being thrust on top of the lower one [9,10]. Basalts, tuffaceous conglom- erates and ~ 800 m thick sandstones bearing Inoceramus of Campanian age (Matakatan For- mation) are exposed at the base of the lower complex. These rocks are conformably overlain by unmetamorphozed tuffaceous siltstones and sandstones of the Malokuril Formation, which is ~ 400 m thick and bears the Maastrichtian species of Inoceramus [11]. The upper thrust sheet con- sists mainly of ophiolites, and is overlain by Maastrichtian-Paleocene conglomerates [12]. On the Nemuro Peninsula
