e Paris, Paris, France e U.S. Geological Survey, Denver, CO, USA Received 10 February 1994; revision accepted 15 May 1994 Abstract The lower Eocene Willwood Formation in the Bighorn Basin of Wyoming preserves a rich and diverse mammalian and floral record. The paleomagnetic behavior of the sequence of floodplain paleosols of varying degrees of maturation ranges from excellent to poor. We present a magnetostratigraphic section for a composite section near Worland, Wyoming, by using a set of strict criteria for interpreting the step-wise alternating field and thermal demagnetization data of 266 samples from 90 sites throughout the composite section. Correlation to the geomagnetic reversal time scale was achieved by combining magnetostratigraphic and biostratigraphic data from this section, from a section in the Clark's Fork Basin in northern Wyoming, and from DSDP Site 550, with the isotopic date determined on a tuff near the top of our section. Our correlation suggests that the Bighorn Basin composite section in the Worland area spans from within Chron C24r to near the top of Chron C24n, or from approximately 55 to 52 Ma. This correlation places the Paleocene/Eocene boundary within the vicinity of the base of the section. Cryptochron C24r.6 of Cande and Kent is tentative

on a tuff near the top of our section. Our correlation suggests that the Bighorn Basin composite section in the Worland area spans from within Chron C24r to near the top of Chron C24n, or from approximately 55 to 52 Ma. This correlation places the Paleocene/Eocene boundary within the vicinity of the base of the section. Cryptochron C24r.6 of Cande and Kent is tentatively identified some 100 m above the base of the section. The temporal framework provided here enables correlation of the mammalian biostratigraphy of the Bighorn Basin to other continental sequences as well as to marine records. It also provides independent chronological information for the calculation of sediment accumulation rates to constrain soil maturation rates. We exclude an age as young as 53 Ma for the Paleocene/Eocene boundary and support older ages, as recommended in recent time scales. The location of a tuff dated at 52.8 + 0.3 Ma at the older boundary C24n.1 is consistent with the age of 52.5 Ma estimated by Cande and Kent and inconsistent with that of 53.7 Ma, from Harland et al. Primary thermoremanence has been demonstrated in samples from 23 sites in a tilted Cretaceous-Palaeogene lava sequence in the Balantak ophiolite at Batusimpang on the eastern tip of the East Arm of Sulawesi. Its direction (D = 60.5 °, I = -32.1 °, a95 = 5.5 °) indicates formation at 17 + 4°S and ~ 60 ° of subsequent clockwise rotation. Introduction The tectonically active regions between Asia and Australia are of general geological interest because they are the site of perhaps the most spectacular convergence and accretion of crust that is currently occurring anywhere on Earth. An understanding of the present-day geology and tectonics together with the unravelling of their development over the last 100 m.y. constitute a model scenario that should throw light on the [RvdV] evolution of older plate convergence zones. The region is large and immensely complex and the evidence is both fragmentary and obscure, and hence the whole range of available geoscientific techniques needs to be used in order to recon- struct its history. Geological evidence indicates that fragments in the tectonic mosaic

orded by Late Miocene volcanic rocks of the Southwest Arm are indistinguishable from those of Earth's present magnetic field. The palaeo- magnetic results from SW Sulawesi are very simi- lar to those from Cretaceous rocks of the Malay Peninsula [7] and Borneo [8], suggesting little latitudinal movement between these areas and similar anticlockwise rotations since the Late Mesozoic and before the Late Miocene. Otofuji et al. [9] suggested that the North Arm of Su- lawesi has rotated clockwise by more than 90 ° with no significant latitude change since the Eocene-Early Miocene, but their data are insuf- ficient to justify any such conclusion. ODP Leg 124 drilling in the Celebes Sea indicated no sig- nificant difference from present-day latitude, but about a 60 ° anticlockwise rotation between the late Eocene and Early Miocene. 3. In some areas there is a transition to the sheeted complex. On the coast of the East Arm there is a faulted contact between sheeted dykes and basalts. Most of the basalts are porphyritic with phenocrysts of plagioclase and pyroxene in a glassy matrix con- taining microlites of plagioclase, pyroxene and magnetite and they commonly contain amygdales up to 2.5 cm across, filled by zeolites and/or calcite. The basalts are typically highly altered with plagioclase replaced by zeolites, saussurite and carbonate; pyroxene is replaced by chlorite, epidote, iron oxides and rarely hornblende; olivine is altered to serpentine; and glass is partially devitrified. In parts of the East Arm sedimentary rocks are tectonically associated with ophiolitic rocks. Introduction The tectonically active regions between Asia and Australia are of general geological interest because they are the site of perhaps the most spectacular convergence and accretion of crust that is currently occurring anywhere on Earth. An understanding of the present-day geology and tectonics together with the unravelling of their development over the last 100 m.y. constitute a model scenario that should throw light on the [RvdV] evolution of older plate convergence zones. The region is large and immensely complex and the evidence is both fragmentary and obscure, and hence the whole range of available geoscientific techniques needs to be used in order to recon- struct its history. Geological evidence indicates that fragments in the tectonic mosaic

orded by Late Miocene volcanic rocks of the Southwest Arm are indistinguishable from those of Earth's present magnetic field. The palaeo- magnetic results from SW Sulawesi are very simi- lar to those from Cretaceous rocks of the Malay Peninsula [7] and Borneo [8], suggesting little latitudinal movement between these areas and similar anticlockwise rotations since the Late Mesozoic and before the Late Miocene. Otofuji et al. [9] suggested that the North Arm of Su- lawesi has rotated clockwise by more than 90 ° with no significant latitude change since the Eocene-Early Miocene, but their data are insuf- ficient to justify any such conclusion. ODP Leg 124 drilling in the Celebes Sea indicated no sig- nificant difference from present-day latitude, but about a 60 ° anticlockwise rotation between the late Eocene and Early Miocene. 3. Introduction The tectonically active regions between Asia and Australia are of general geological interest because they are the site of perhaps the most spectacular convergence and accretion of crust that is currently occurring anywhere on Earth. An understanding of the present-day geology and tectonics together with the unravelling of their development over the last 100 m.y. constitute a model scenario that should throw light on the [RvdV] evolution of older plate convergence zones. The region is large and immensely complex and the evidence is both fragmentary and obscure, and hence the whole range of available geoscientific techniques needs to be used in order to recon- struct its history. Geological evidence indicates that fragments in the tectonic mosaic

e western volcanic arc [e.g., 1-4], resulting in ophiolite emplacement and metamorphism. How- ever, as work in the region has progressed it has become clear that this apparent simplicity is partly a reflection of the incomplete knowledge of a large area which is remote, mountainous and largely covered by thick rainforest. In particular, little is known of the age and origin of the East Sulawesi ophiolite, which is likely to have formed far from its present position. 2. Previous palaeomagnetic work There has been little previous palaeomagnetic work on Sulawesi. The earliest results were re- ported by Haile [5] from oriented block samples of cherts from the Southwest and Southeast Arms. They indicated that these arms were situated in different palaeogeographic regions during the Late Jurassic-Early Cretaceous, as proposed by Audley-Charles et al. [2] and Katili [3]. Data from SW Sulawesi indicate that the Southwest Arm has remained close to its present latitude since the Late Jurassic [5] and late Paleogene [6] but has rotated anticlockwise by about 45 °. Directions recorded by Late Miocene volcanic rocks of the Southwest Arm are indistinguishable from those of Earth's present magnetic field. Since then, more poles for the Yangtze Block have been published, with some of the most reliable results coming from the Mesozoic (e.g. Linet al., 1985; Opdyke et al., 1986; Heller et al., 1988; Steiner et al., 1989). The most recent and comprehensive APWP for Yangtze from the Permian to the Present, was published by Enkin et al. (1992), incorporating and critically evaluating the results to date. The problems of remagnetization and working in a tectonically disturbed area, however, have hampered refinement of the APWP for this block. Although the Mesozoic has been studied in perhaps the most detail - the Triassic in particular - there are still few reliable poles reported in the literature. This scarcity of reported poles for south China from the Mesozoic and large statistical ambiguities have resulted in an APWP with large confidence limits in which the trend of the pole path is emerging but the detail is still lacking. Since then, more poles for the Yangtze Block have been published, with some of the most reliable results coming from the Mesozoic (e.g. Linet al., 1985; Opdyke et al., 1986; Heller et al., 1988; Steiner et al., 1989). The most recent and comprehensive APWP for Yangtze from the Permian to the Present, was published by Enkin et al. (1992), incorporating and critically evaluating the results to date. The problems of remagnetization and working in a tectonically disturbed area, however, have hampered refinement of the APWP for this block. Although the Mesozoic has been studied in perhaps the most detail - the Triassic in particular - there are still few reliable poles reported in the literature. This scarcity of reported poles for south China from the Mesozoic and large statistical ambiguities have resulted in an APWP with large confidence limits in which the trend of the pole path is emerging but the detail is still lacking. The large A95 of the Middle to Late Triassic pole position (Enkin et al., 1992), however, and the recent discrepancies of Triassic results for the Yangtze Block (Steiner et al., 1989; Dobson and Heller, 1993) mean that a post-folding, Middle to Late Triassic remagnetization should not be completely ruled out. The question then arises - why are the Yinkeng sediments apparently unaffected by the remagnetization that affected the Changxing Formation? Results of the IRM studies reveal that the only significant difference in the magnetic minerals from the two formations is the presence of goethite in the Yinkeng Formation. There is evidence for the presence of magnetite as well as hematite in both formations, though the relative abundances and grain sizes may play a role in the stability of the signals. The overlapping of the blocking temperature spectra, however, make it difficult to determine the relative contributions of each (Figure 4). All of the stable Yinkeng samples come from the dolomitic layers in the section, while the samples from the Changxing Formation and the unstable Yinkeng samples come from limestones. The overlapping of the blocking temperature spectra, however, make it difficult to determine the relative contributions of each (Figure 4). All of the stable Yinkeng samples come from the dolomitic layers in the section, while the samples from the Changxing Formation and the unstable Yinkeng samples come from limestones. The only difference seen in the IRM experiments between the dolomites and limestones is reflected in the presence of goethite in the dolomites. Its origin is unclear. It seems then, that the dolomitization of these sediments may be responsible for the preservation of the Early Triassic magnetization since the formation of dolomite can, in many cases, greatly decrease the porosity of a rock unit. This reduction in porosity may have prevented fluids responsible for the Jurassic remagnetization events from passing through the dolomite, thus enabling the preservation of the Early Triassic signal in those sediments. Paleomagnetic and rock magnetic experiments on the Triassic Yinkeng Formation and the Permian Changxing Formation sampled from the Permian-Triassic type section, Changxing County, reveal that a high temperature primary direction is isolated in dolomitic samples from the Early Triassic but the Late Permian limestones samples appear to be remagnetized during the Jurassic. A Permian-Triassic pole previously reported for the Changxing Formation from this section (Linet al., 1985) is not in agreement with results from this study or other poles for that time interval reported for the Yangtze Block and may be remagnetized. Introduction The Changxing Permian-Triassic type section is located in the Baoqing Quarry, Changxing County, about 80 km north of Hangzhou (Figure 1). Exposed in the quarry is 50 meters of irregularly bedded greyish limestones with some inte

(Figure 1). Exposed in the quarry is 50 meters of irregularly bedded greyish limestones with some interbedded grey mudstones and shales, and dolomites and limestones in the late part of the Yinkeng Formation. The boundary between the Late Permian Changxing Formation and the Early Triassic Yinkeng is marked by a greyish- yellowish boundary clay layer. The section was sampled by Lin and others (1985) and the results were used in the calculation of a Permian-Triassic pole for the Yangtze Block. This section was also sampled by Li and Wang (1987) and they were able to resolve a magnetic stratigraphy though Lin (1984) reported only one polarity from the section. Recently it has been shown that Lin's pole from the Changxing section may be remagnetized (Steiner et al., 1989; Dobson and Mauritsch, 1989). In the most recent and comprehensive compilation of Chinese results from the Permian to Present, Enkin et al. (1992) use the results from 16 samples at the very top of this section (from the study of Li and Wang) in calculations of a mean Early Triassic paleopole for the Yangtze Block. Introduction The Changxing Permian-Triassic type section is located in the Baoqing Quarry, Changxing County, about 80 km north of Hangzhou (Figure 1). Exposed in the quarry is 50 meters of irregularly bedded greyish limestones with some interbedded grey mudstones and shales, and dolomites and limestones in the late part of the Yinkeng Formation. The boundary between the Late Permian Changxing Formation and the Early Triassic Yinkeng is marked by a greyish- yellowish boundary clay layer. The section was sampled by Lin and others (1985) and the results were used in the calculation of a Permian-Triassic pole for the Yangtze Block. In the most recent and comprehensive compilation of Chinese results from the Permian to Present, Enkin et al. These were the only results from outside of the south-central Sichuan Province area used by Enkin et al. (1992) in the calculation of the Early Triassic direction for the block and are, therefore, very important. For this reason, we present here new results from our study of the Changxing section and examine the rock magnetic properties of samples from the section. We infer, therefore, that the pillow basalts of the Vizcaino Norte and Sur terranes were remagnetized in middle Cretaceous time after they had been juxtaposed and deformed, probably within a subduction zone. Because structural deformation preceeded remagnetization, paleohorizontal and hence the paleolatitude at which these rocks were accreted to the continental margin cannot be determined. The objectives of the studies were threefold. The first objective was to contrib- ute to the data base for western Newfoundland that provides evidence of various motions involved in the closing of the Iapetus Ocean during the Paleozoic. The geology of the island of Newfoundland has been interpreted over the past 25 years as resulting from the opening and closing of an early Paleozoic Iapetus Ocean (Wilson 1966; Williams et al. 1972; Williams 1979 and references therein; McKerrow and Scotese 1990; Williams 1992). Apart from the rotations of western New- foundland relative to cratonic North America that were sug- Printed in Canada / Imprimt au Canada gested by Black (1964), western Newfoundland has always been considered part of cratonic North America. A compari- son of western Newfoundland paleomagnetic data with data of contemporaneous rocks from Avalonia would provide reason- able constraints on the suggested motions at the time of the closing of the Iapetus Ocean. The second objective was to establish whether the red sand- stone units on eithe

Geology and sampling Williams (1979) summarized the geology of the island of Newfoundland in the broader context of the tectonics of the Appalachian orogen. Four distinct lithotectonic zones were recognized; from west to east, these were the Humber, Dunnage, Gander, and Avalon zones. The Port au Port Penin- sula, in the Humber Zone, has been extensively studied geo- logically (Schuchert and Dunbar 1934; Sullivan 1940; Riley 1962; Rodgers and Neale 1963; Rodgers 1965; Fahraeus 1973; O'Brien 1975; Dean 1979; Williams 1985). interest in the present study are the coastal exposures of red sandstones between Misty Point and Red Point on either side of Lourdes Cove (Fig. 1). In most of the literature cited above, they are described as part of the Clam Bank Formation. They comprise mostly brick-red sandstone and mudstone. The sandstones exhibit cross-bedding and are commonly coarse grained. Units of fine-grained sandstone and siltstone alternate with mudstone and coarse-grained sand- stone. At the north end of Lourdes Cove, rocks of the Clam Bank Formation conformably overlie the grey sandstones of the Middle Ordovician Long Point Group (Rodgers 1965; Williams 1985). At the south end of Lourdes Cove, Rodgers (1965) recognized Siluro-Devonian brachiopods in grey shales and sandstones of the Clam Bank Formation. Along Long Point, the Clam Bank Formation and the upper member of the Long Point Group are homoclinal. Strata of the two forma- tions strike at approximately 240" and dip at 40-50" NW. From about 2 km northeast of Lourdes to Red Point, all expo- sures dip southeast, sometimes by as much as 80". Earth Sci. 30, 776-786 (1993) Objectives Paleomagnetic studies have been carried out on red sand- stone beds exposed on either side of Lourdes Cove, Port au Port peninsula, in western Newfoundland. The objectives of the studies were threefold. The first objective was to contrib- ute to the data base for western Newfoundland that provides evidence of various motions involved in the closing of the Iapetus Ocean during the Paleozoic. The geology of the island of Newfoundland has been interpreted over the past 25 years as resulting from the opening and closing of an early Paleozoic Iapetus Ocean (Wilson 1966; Williams et al. 1972; Williams 1979 and references therein; McKerrow and Scotese 1990; Williams 1992). Apart from the rotations of western New- foundland relative to cratonic North America that were sug- Printed in Canada / Imprimt au Canada gested by Black (1964), western Newfoundland has always been considered part of cratonic North America. A compari- son of western Newfoundland paleomagnetic data with data of contemporaneous rocks from Avalonia would provide reason- able constraints on the suggested motions at the time of the closing of the Iapetus Ocean. The second objective was to establish whether the red sand- stone units on eithe

A compari- son of western Newfoundland paleomagnetic data with data of contemporaneous rocks from Avalonia would provide reason- able constraints on the suggested motions at the time of the closing of the Iapetus Ocean. The Port au Port Penin- sula, in the Humber Zone, has been extensively studied geo- logically (Schuchert and Dunbar 1934; Sullivan 1940; Riley 1962; Rodgers and Neale 1963; Rodgers 1965; Fahraeus 1973; O'Brien 1975; Dean 1979; Williams 1985). interest in the present study are the coastal exposures of red sandstones between Misty Point and Red Point on either side of Lourdes Cove (Fig. 1). In most of the literature cited above, they are described as part of the Clam Bank Formation. They comprise mostly brick-red sandstone and mudstone. The sandstones exhibit cross-bedding and are commonly coarse grained. Units of fine-grained sandstone and siltstone alternate with mudstone and coarse-grained sand- stone. At the north end of Lourdes Cove, rocks of the Clam Bank Formation conformably overlie the grey sandstones of the Middle Ordovician Long Point Group (Rodgers 1965; Williams 1985). At the south end of Lourdes Cove, Rodgers (1965) recognized Siluro-Devonian brachiopods in grey shales and sandstones of the Clam Bank Formation. Along Long Point, the Clam Bank Formation and the upper member of the Long Point Group are homoclinal. Strata of the two forma- tions strike at approximately 240" and dip at 40-50" NW. From about 2 km northeast of Lourdes to Red Point, all expo- sures dip southeast, sometimes by as much as 80". The median natural remanent magnetization intensity from 509 specimens from 40 sites is 3.6 X A/m. This intensity is an order of magnitude lower than most MVT deposits and is close to the sensitivity of the cryo- genic magnetometer, so only the stronger specimens could be analysed paleomagnetically . Isothermal remanent magnetization testing of ores, host rocks, and monomineralic specimens shows that single domain to pseudosingle domain magnetite in sphalerite is the main remanence carrier; magnetite in galena is the next most significant carrier. In contrast, barren dolostone, limestone, and calcite crystals have a much weaker remanence. Using less stringent criteria than is conventional, 17 acceptable site mean remanence directions were determined. Remagnetization circle data indicate that many of the poorly defined sites retain a reversed but nonisolated characteristic remanence. The A pole indicates with >95% confidence that the MVT ores at Pine Point are Late Cretaceous to Eocene in age, with a mid-Late Cretaceous to Paleocene age (84 -58 Ma) being most likely. Stable remanence directions in each specimen were obtained using stereographic, intensity decay and orthogonal demagne- tization diagrams and least squares principal component analy- sis (Kirschvink 1980). Directions of remanence were accepted with a maximum angle of deviation (MAD) of < 10". Site mean remanence directions were calcu- lated using two-tiered statistics (Fisher 1953; Watson and Irving 1957). Tectonic analysis of the relative rotations (RR's) (RR's < 0 indicate clockwise rotation) and the relative paleolatitudinal displacements (RPD's) (RPD's > 0 indicate northward paleo- latitudinal displacement) with respect to cratonic North America were calculated by the method of Yole and Irving (1980, 1981), incorporating the error analysis of Demarest (1983). The dominant down-west mag- netization was described in a number of studies including Strangway (1961), Fahrig et al. A second rernanence (herein called the Senneterre remanence) has been reported in the literature at only four sites. It was recognized as an up-north magnetization by Larochelle (1966) at three sampling sites in two dykes, and as a magnetization of opposite polarity by Symons et al. (1981) at a single site. Preliminary unpublished work (W.F. Fahrig, personal com- munication 1985) indicated that this magnetization occurs in other northeast-trending quartz tholeiite ,dykes. Finally, a third shallow south-southwest remanence direc- tion was obtained by Larochelle (1966) at four sites from a single dyke. eissac dykes. It is demonstrated that they are readily separated on the basis of paleomagnetism into subsets, referred to as the Biscotasing and Senneterre swarms. In addition a pair of unnamed dykes may be associated with the north- and northwest-trending Matachewan swarm farther west. Biscotasing dykes have a down-west magnetization of single polarity with a corresponding paleopole at 27.8'N, 136.7"W (dm = 12.3" and dp = 9.4"). Most samples contained one or two magnetic components. The first component removed is usually a minor secondary mag- netization of northerly declination and moderate positive incli- nation and is aligned approximately subparallel with the Earth's present field direction. This magnetization is com- monly removed by AF demagnetization of 5 - 10 mT and by thermal demagnetization in temperatures less than 300°C. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: 1, 1993 Paleomagnetic samples were collected from Mid-Pennsylvanian to Lower Permian red argillaceous cherts at two localities of the Slide Mountain terrane: 18 sites from the Sylvester allochthon in northern British Columbia and 11 sites from Sliding Mountain in central British Columbia. A secondary component of natural remanent magnetization in the Sylvester samples yields a paleomagnetic pole that can be brought into coincidence with the Jurassic portion of the North American apparent polar wander path by inferring vertical-axis rotation during obduction of the allochthon. Both localities yield a characteristic component (ChRM) with unblocking temperatures from 650 to 680°C. After structural correction for bedding tilt, all inclina- tions of ChRM are negative, consistent with magnetization during a reversed-polarity interval in the northern hemisphere. Site-mean ChRM directions show consistent inclinations but distinct stratigraphic groupings of declinations. Inclination-only statistics indicate that the ChRM passes a tilt test within the Sylvester allochthon and regionally between the two localities. The ChRM was apparently acquired prior to structural imbrication within the Sylvester section and regional differential tilting. We interpret the ChRM to be a primary magnetization acquired

he origin of Uairen sediments is believed to be fluvial. They comprise conglomerates, sandstones, quartzites, quart- zose sandstones, and indurated sandstones. Intraformational conglomerates are common in the lowest part of the forma- tion: These are of economic importance, since diamonds and gold are found in streams that drain the conglomerates. Thin-section analyses of vertical and horizontal cuts of the Uairen sediments sampled for this study reveal a large amount (between 70 and 90 %) of quartz cemented by authigenic seri- cite and muscovite cemented by sericite. These samples are stained with iron hydroxide and they also show hematite, feld- spar, illite, zircon, microcline, apatite, epidote, and magne- tite. X-ray diffraction analyses revealed, in decreasing order of concentration, quartz, muscovite, feldspar, hematite, illite, magnetite, zircon, apatite, epidote, chlorite, tourmaline, pie- montite, and kaolinite. Previous paleomagnetic studies of these lava flows, known collectively as the Lake Shore Traps, have produced contradictory results. To investigate the cause of these conflicting results, 30 sites encompassing the most complete section of lava flows possible were collected and analyzed. Well-defined characteristic directions of magnetization were isolated using either alternating-field or thermal demagnetiza- tion or a combination of both. These directions of magnetization are interpreted as primary magnetizations acquired during the original cooling of the lavas. Hysteresis, thermomagnetic, and petrographic analyses suggest the carrier of magnetization is a pseudo-single-domain, titanium-poor magnetite that has undergone some high-temperature oxidation. Site means determined from the 30 lava flows define three distinct directional clusters. Each cluster of directions cor- responds to a different stratigraphic package of lava flows with the Copper Harbor Conglomerate. Between-site dispersion for each stratigraphic package or unit is much less than the expected value for Keweenawan-age rocks. Therefore, we suggest that most of the lava flows in each unit were extruded rapidly and that within an individual st

been adequately sampled. This explains why previous studies on the Lake Shore Traps have produced such different results; each study did not sample the entire range of directions possible in these lava flows. The paleomagnetic pole calculated from the 30 site-mean virtual geomagnetic poles is located at 22.2ON, 180.8"E (k = 35.0; A,, = 6.5"). The new Copper Harbor pole is now located in the appropriate chronological position with respect to the underlying Portage Lake Volcanics and the overlying Nonesuch Shale on the Keweenawan apparent polar wander path. The similarity of our Copper Harbor pole to that of the Portage Lake Volcanics reinforces the idea that the Copper Harbor Conglomerate is more closely related in time to the Portage Lake Volcanics than to the Nonesuch Shale. The unit is a reddish-brown, coarsely stratified pebble to boulder conglomerate with thin sandstone interbeds in its lower portion; higher in the section sandstone becomes the dominate facies. Conglomerate clasts are primarily rhyolitic, with approximately 10% being basal- tic. The thickness of the Copper Harbor Conglomerate ranges from 200 to 2000 m (White and Wright 1960; Daniels 1982), thickening toward the Lake Superior basin. White and Wright (1960) and more recently Elmore (1984) have interpreted the Copper Harbor Conglomerate as coalesced alluvial fans and sand flats deposited by northward-flowing streams originating from hills along the southern margin of the Lake Superior basin. The Copper Harbor Conglomerate interfingers with and conformably overlies the Portage Lake Volcanics, a 2500 - 5200 m series of subaerial flood basalts dated at approximately 1.1 Ga (White 1960; Van Schmus et al. 1982; Davis and Paces 1990). The Nonesuch Shale interfingers with and conformably overlies the Copper Harbor Conglomerate, which in turn is comformably overlain by the Freda Sandstone. Previous paleomagnetic studies of these lava flows, known collectively as the Lake Shore Traps, have produced contradictory results. To investigate the cause of these conflicting results, 30 sites encompassing the most complete section of lava flows possible were collected and analyzed. These directions of magnetization are interpreted as primary magnetizations acquired during the original cooling of the lavas. Hysteresis, thermomagnetic, and petrographic analyses suggest the carrier of magnetization is a pseudo-single-domain, titanium-poor magnetite that has undergone some high-temperature oxidation. Site means determined from the 30 lava flows define three distinct directional clusters. Each cluster of directions cor- responds to a different stratigraphic package of lava flows with the Copper Harbor Conglomerate. Between-site dispersion for each stratigraphic package or unit is much less than the expected value for Keweenawan-age rocks. Therefore, we suggest that most of the lava flows in

ch unit were extruded rapidly and that within an individual stratigraphic unit, paleosecular variation has not been adequately sampled. This explains why previous studies on the Lake Shore Traps have produced such different results; each study did not sample the entire range of directions possible in these lava flows. The paleomagnetic pole calculated from the 30 site-mean virtual geomagnetic poles is located at 22.2ON, 180.8"E (k = 35.0; A,, = 6.5"). The new Copper Harbor pole is now located in the appropriate chronological position with respect to the underlying Portage Lake Volcanics and the overlying Nonesuch Shale on the Keweenawan apparent polar wander path. The similarity of our Copper Harbor pole to that of the Portage Lake Volcanics reinforces the idea that the Copper Harbor Conglomerate is more closely related in time to the Portage Lake Volcanics than to the Nonesuch Shale. Ramsay (1961) has shown, in the general context of structural geology, that failure to recognize plunges of 30" or less leads only to small errors in directional estimation (small, that is, by comparison with confidence limits commonly associated with palaeomagnetic results). We have completed a paleomagnetic reconnaissance study of sedimentary and volcanic extrusive rocks collected from two major tectonic zones in northeastern Russia. Paleomagnetic sites were sampled within the fault-bounded structural units of the Khatyrka and Maynitsky superterranes and an overlap sequence of the Khatyrka superterrane. These sampling localities were chosen to allow both within-site and between-site fold tests. Stepwise thermal demagnetization within the temperature range ZOO-640°C showed a characteristic linear demagneti~tion path between thermal demagnetization steps of 400°C and SWC. For thermal steps above 55O”C, the magnetic intensity of many samples began to increase rapidly with magnetic directions, which were random between heating steps, suggesting the formation of new magnetic phases in these samples. Paleomagnetic samples collected from basalts and sediments of the Khatyrka superterrane and basalts and gabbros of the Maynitsky superterrane pass fold tests and show significant poleward motion of these superterranes since the formation of their rocks. The observed paleomagnetic paleolatitudes between 24”N or S and 32”N or S can be compared with expected paleolatitudes of 57”N to 79”N.
